Q: Explanation of numbers in Haskell A:

This answer mostly assumes you know the difference between types and type classes. If that difference is hazy to you then clear up your understanding there before reading on.

Num

Num is a typeclass that includes all numeric types.

:info Num
class Num a where
  (+) :: a -> a -> a
  (-) :: a -> a -> a
  (*) :: a -> a -> a
  negate :: a -> a
  abs :: a -> a
  signum :: a -> a
  fromInteger :: Integer -> a
        -- Defined in ‘GHC.Num’
instance Num Word -- Defined in ‘GHC.Num’
instance Num Integer -- Defined in ‘GHC.Num’
instance Num Int -- Defined in ‘GHC.Num’
instance Num Float -- Defined in ‘GHC.Float’
instance Num Double -- Defined in ‘GHC.Float’

Real

Also a typeclass covering those types that can be represented as a real value (the Rational type).

:info Real
class (Num a, Ord a) => Real a where
  toRational :: a -> Rational
        -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Real Word -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Real Integer -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Real Int -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Real Float -- Defined in ‘GHC.Float’
instance Real Double -- Defined in ‘GHC.Float’

Integral

A type class for integrals, you know, ...,-2,-1,0,1,.... Types such as Integer (aka big int), Int, Int64, etc are instances.

:info Integral
class (Real a, Enum a) => Integral a where
  quot :: a -> a -> a
  rem :: a -> a -> a
  div :: a -> a -> a
  mod :: a -> a -> a
  quotRem :: a -> a -> (a, a)
  divMod :: a -> a -> (a, a)
  toInteger :: a -> Integer
        -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Integral Word -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Integral Integer -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’
instance Integral Int -- Defined in ‘GHC.Real’

Integer

A type, not a type class such as what we've talked about till now, that can represent unbounded integers. So 2^3028 is a legal value.

Int

A fixed-width integral. In the GHC compiler this is 32 or 64 bits depending on your architecture. The Haskell language only guarantees this will be at least 29 bits.

Ratio

This is a type constructor, so you would say something like Ratio Integer to get a type for ratio's of two integers (mathematically a/b).

Rational

Well a rational is literally a ratio of two integers, understand ratio and you're good:

:i Rational
type Rational = Ratio Integer

Double

A type for double precision floating point values.

Float

A type for single precision floating point values.

Q: RegEx Find all words that are NOT in line with a starting Single Quote A:

If in your use case it is OK to extract matches from a submatch (i.e. a capture group), then you could use this pattern:

(?:^'.*$\s*|^(?!.*\b(?:Set|CreateObject|Open)\b).*$\s*)*.*?\b(Set|CreateObject|Open)\b

This greedily looks for complete lines that either start with a single quote or don't have any of the targeted words, arriving at a position outside such lines, and from there looks on that line for a targeted keyword, but it does not include those preceding lines and characters in the capture group.

Here is a script using that pattern on your example input:

Dim txt, regex, matches, word, index

txt = "'Open is a Set line word" & vbCrLf & _
      "Here is the word Set we want CreateObject" & vbCrLf & _
      "'CreateObject quoted Set word" & vbCrLf & _
      "Open also has the word"

Set regex = CreateObject("VBScript.RegExp")
regex.IgnoreCase = False
regex.Global = True
regex.Multiline = True
regex.Pattern = "(?:^'.*$\s*|^(?!.*\b(?:Set|CreateObject|Open)\b).*$\s*)*.*?\b(Set|CreateObject|Open)\b"

Set matches = regex.Execute(txt)
For Each match In matches
    word = match.SubMatches(0)  ' This is the match you look for
    ' In case you need its offset in the original string...
    index = match.FirstIndex + Len(match.Value) - Len(word)
    Response.Write "Found '" & word & "' at index " & index & "<br>"
Next

This will output (in a browser):

Found 'Set' at index 43
Found 'CreateObject' at index 55
Found 'Open' at index 100

Use of Replace

If the goal is to replace the matched words, like wrapping them in asterisks, then you can use Replace. You'll have to capture the first part of the regex in a capture group as well, so you can reproduce it in the replace string:

regex.Pattern = "((?:^'.*$\s*|^(?!.*\b(?:Set|CreateObject|Open)\b).*$\s*)*.*?)\b(Set|CreateObject|Open)\b"

txt = regex.Replace(txt, "$1*$2*")

This will update the text to this:

'Open is a Set line word
Here is the word *Set* we want *CreateObject*
'CreateObject quoted Set word
*Open* also has the word

Q: I'm experiencing slow download times for videos from Telegram using GramJS with the Downloadmedia method A:

Yes — with GramJS the biggest “free” win is parallelism. Right now you’re forcing workers: 1, which is the slowest setting.

1) Speed up downloadMedia (most important)

Increase workers (parallel chunk downloads). GramJS explicitly supports this, and warns that >16 is unstable.

const buffer = await client.downloadMedia(message.media, {

workers: 8, // try 4, 8, 12, 16

});

Practical tips:

  • Start with 8. If your CPU/network can handle it, try 12–16.

  • If you download many files, you may get better throughput by downloading multiple files concurrently (each with fewer workers), instead of one file with max workers.
